Accrual, dropout and the choice of endpoints

Source: vignettes/trial-settings.Rmd
trial-settings.Rmd
library(CorOncoEndpoints)
ctl <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.40, death.prop = 0.15,
               os.median = 15, pps.hr.resp = 0.6)
trt <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6 / 0.7, orr = 0.45, resp.cor = 0.40,
               death.prop = 0.15, pps.hazard = ctl$gam0, pps.hr.resp = 0.6)
arms <- list(Control = ctl, Treatment = trt)

This vignette shows how the settings of a trial are specified: accrual, dropout and the censoring of PFS, the observation of response, groups with two of the three endpoints, and random-number streams for simulations run in batches. Time is in months throughout.

Accrual

Accrual is specified as in the FastSurvival package. a.time gives the breakpoints of the accrual intervals, and the number of patients in each interval is given by rates in patients per month (a.rate) or by proportions (a.prop). The rates refer to all groups together. The number of patients of each group in each interval is fixed, and the patients are placed uniformly within their interval.

With one more rate than intervals, the last rate applies to an open final interval that ends when all patients are enrolled. Below, 10 patients per month are enrolled for 6 months and then 30 per month until the 300 patients are enrolled.

d1 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(150, 150), arms = arms,
                     a.time = c(0, 6), a.rate = c(10, 30), seed = 1)
table(interval = cut(d1$accrual_time, c(0, 6, Inf), right = FALSE), d1$group)
#>          
#> interval  Control Treatment
#>   [0,6)        30        30
#>   [6,Inf)     120       120
max(d1$accrual_time)
#> [1] 13.99021

The first 6 months enroll 60 patients, 30 per group, and accrual ends at month 14. With as many rates as intervals, the rates must accrue the total sample size; otherwise an error suggests the alternatives. Proportions describe the same pattern without rates:

d2 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(150, 150), arms = arms,
                     a.time = c(0, 6, 14), a.prop = c(0.2, 0.8), seed = 2)
table(interval = cut(d2$accrual_time, c(0, 6, 14), right = FALSE), d2$group)
#>         
#> interval Control Treatment
#>   [0,6)       30        30
#>   [6,14)     120       120

Accrual may start after time 0, for example for the patients of the expansion of a trial. Here 20 patients per month are enrolled from month 12:

d3 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(50, 50), arms = arms, a.time = 12,
                     a.rate = 20, seed = 3)
range(d3$accrual_time)
#> [1] 12.06227 16.95176

ExpectedEvents(), AverageHR() and RequiredEvents() take the same arguments:

ExpectedEvents(arms, n = c(150, 150), a.time = c(0, 6), a.rate = c(10, 30),
               endpoint = "os", time = c(12, 24, 36))
#>   time    events   Control Treatment
#> 1   12  28.49156  16.26906  12.22251
#> 2   24 136.73264  75.49925  61.23340
#> 3   36 215.87670 115.12934 100.74737

Dropout and censoring of PFS

Dropout is exponential with hazard d.hazard (or median d.median) and censors PFS and OS. A proportion q lost to follow-up within a year corresponds to the hazard -log(1 - q) / 12 per month. Piecewise exponential dropout is given by hazards in d.hazard and breakpoints in d.time.

pfs.cens.hazard adds a censoring time that applies to PFS only, for example the start of another anticancer therapy before progression, after which OS is still followed. Both censoring mechanisms are independent of the endpoints.

q <- 0.05
d4 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(2000, 2000), arms = arms, a.time = c(0, 12),
                     d.hazard = -log(1 - q) / 12, pfs.cens.hazard = 0.02, seed = 4)
c(dropout_within_a_year = mean(d4$dropout_time <= 12),
  pfs_censored_by_therapy = mean(d4$pfs_cens_time < pmin(d4$pfs_time, d4$dropout_time)),
  os_events = mean(d4$os_event))
#>   dropout_within_a_year pfs_censored_by_therapy               os_events 
#>                 0.04425                 0.16425                 0.90975
d5 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = c(2000, 2000), arms = arms, a.time = c(0, 12),
                     d.hazard = c(0.02, 0.005), d.time = c(0, 12, Inf), seed = 5)
c(dropout_before_12 = mean(d5$dropout_time <= 12), expected = 1 - exp(-0.02 * 12))
#> dropout_before_12          expected 
#>         0.2160000         0.2133721

Observation of response

The column response of the generated data is the response of the patient, whether or not it would be observed. CutoffData() decides which responses are observed at an analysis. With resp.timing = "landmark", the response is determined at the first tumor assessment resp.tau, and it is observed only if the patient is still followed then; with resp.timing = "ttr" the time to response plays this role. In response_obs, a patient without an observed response counts as a non-responder, as in an intention-to-treat analysis, and response_eval indicates the patients who were followed up to the first assessment, for an analysis restricted to them.

lm_arm <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.40, death.prop = 0.15,
                  os.median = 15, resp.timing = "landmark", resp.tau = 1.5)
d6 <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = 20000, arms = lm_arm, a.time = c(0, 12),
                     d.hazard = 0.05, seed = 6)
c6 <- CutoffData(d6, cutoff = 24)
c(response = mean(c6$response), observed_itt = mean(c6$response_obs),
  observed_among_assessed = mean(c6$response_obs[c6$response_eval == 1]))
#>                response            observed_itt observed_among_assessed 
#>               0.3050000               0.2837000               0.3058925

Because dropout is independent of response, the proportion among the patients who were assessed estimates the response rate of 0.3, whereas the intention-to-treat proportion is expected to be 0.3 times the probability of being followed up to month 1.5, that is, 0.278. The input orr is therefore the response rate without dropout.

Two of the three endpoints

A group can be described by two endpoints through endpoints in OncoArm(); the columns of the third endpoint are then NA. With PFS and OS only, the response inputs are not needed:

po <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 15,
              endpoints = c("pfs", "os"))
CorEndpoints(po)
#> cor.pfs.resp  cor.os.resp   cor.pfs.os pcor.os.resp 
#>           NA           NA    0.6088695           NA

With OS and response only, OS is exponential and is linked to response directly, so that resp.cor is the correlation between OS and response:

osr <- OncoArm(os.median = 15, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.35,
               endpoints = c("os", "response"))
CorEndpoints(osr)
#> cor.pfs.resp  cor.os.resp   cor.pfs.os pcor.os.resp 
#>           NA         0.35           NA           NA
head(rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 1, n = 5, arms = osr, seed = 7)[
  , c("pfs_time", "os_time", "response")])
#>   pfs_time   os_time response
#> 1       NA  6.102199        0
#> 2       NA 18.407025        1
#> 3       NA 32.557469        1
#> 4       NA 78.446937        1
#> 5       NA 10.191542        0

Alternatively, the three endpoints can be generated and PFS ignored. The correlation between OS and response is then a result of the other inputs, here 0.381 for the control group, and OS is not exponential.

Correlation between PFS and OS as input

The proportion of PFS events that are deaths can be replaced by a target correlation between PFS and OS:

pc <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.40, pfs.os.cor = 0.55,
              os.median = 15)
c(death.prop = pc$death.prop, CorEndpoints(pc)["cor.pfs.os"])
#> death.prop cor.pfs.os 
#>  0.2405415  0.5500000

The attainable correlations are limited by the medians: with medians of 6 and 15 months, values above about 0.68 cannot be reached, and OncoArm() then reports the attainable range.

Simulations in batches

A large simulation can be run in batches with the same seed and different values of stream. Each stream is an independent sequence of random numbers, so a batch gives the same data whether the batches are run one after another or in parallel.

batch <- function(b) {
  rOncoEndpoints(nsim = 10, n = c(150, 150), arms = arms, a.time = c(0, 12),
                 seed = 2026, stream = b)
}
identical(batch(1), batch(1))
#> [1] TRUE
identical(batch(1)$pfs_time, batch(2)$pfs_time)
#> [1] FALSE
